newsitem.title: NORWAY: Statoil begins CO2 injection at Sleipner West.
newsitem.headline: Statoil begins CO2 injection at Sleipner West.

text.p: Den norske stats oljeselskap AS (Statoil) said on Wednesday it had begun injecting carbon dioxide (CO2) 1,000 metres below the seabed at the Sleipner West gas and condensate field.
The project is the largest development to inject CO2 -- involving about one million tonnes per year of the gas -- and is the first time it has been injected at an offshore platform.
The Sleipner West development in the North Sea came on stream at the end of August, one month ahead of schedule and 2.6 billion crowns under budget.
A special feature of Sleipner West's gas is a high CO2 content, which has to be reduced to meet sales specifications before being piped to European customers.

Sleipner West comprises two platforms, the unmanned Sleipner B wellhead unit and the T gas treatment installation. After production the gas is piped to the T-platform, where it is treated to reduce the CO2 content to around 2.5 percent from nine percent.
The stripped CO2 is then injected into a water-bearing structure in Utsira formation sands. The process eliminates the majority of CO2 emissions into the air.

Statoil's Sleipner West is seen as a landmark development as oil companies around the world face tougher environmental regulations. Already those active on the Norwegian continental shelf pay a tax of about 0.80 crowns per cubic metres of CO2 emitted into the atmosphere during oil and gas production.
Recoverable reserves at Sleipner West are estimated at 127 billion cubic metres of gas and 325 million barrels of condensate and NGLs.
Partners in the field are Statoil as operator with 49.50 percent, Exxon Corp's Esso with 32.24 percent, Norsk Hydro with 8.85 percent, Elf Aquitaine with 8.47 percent and Total SA with 0.94 percent.
